hooks.text: Many scientists once rejected the solar wind as utter nonsense.
Four simple lines of algebra revealed an invisible solar storm.
A million-mile-per-hour wind tears through our solar system constantly.

title: When the Solar Wind Was Nonsense
description: The story of how Eugene Parker's 1958 prediction of a million-mile-per-hour solar wind was initially rejected by the scientific community.

beats.text: Many scientists once rejected the solar wind as utter nonsense.
In 1958, astrophysicist Eugene Parker theorized the Sun’s million-degree corona must expand into space.
beats.visual: Solar corona during a total solar eclipse, photograph

beats.text: Parker noted that the math for this discovery required just four lines of algebra.
beats.visual: Eugene Parker at a blackboard with physics equations

beats.text: He predicted a supersonic torrent of charged particles tearing through the solar system at a million miles per hour.
beats.visual: Diagram of solar wind particles interacting with Earth's magnetosphere

beats.text: When he submitted his findings to a major journal, two reviewers recommended rejection.
beats.visual: The Astrophysical Journal cover page archive

beats.text: Editor [Subrahmanyan](/sˈʌbɹˈɑmˈɑnjˈæn/) [Chandrasekhar](/ʧˈʌndɹˈɑʃˈAkˈɑɹ/) overruled them and published the paper despite his own doubts.
Yet before spacecraft proved this phenomenon was real, many experts believed the space between planets was a perfect vacuum.
beats.visual: Telescopic view of a comet showing a distinct plasma tail

beats.text: Within months, Soviet probe Luna 1 detected the particles, followed by NASA’s Mariner 2 mission.
beats.visual: Artist's concept of the Soviet Luna 1 spacecraft in space

beats.text: This invisible storm now defines our corner of the galaxy.
beats.visual: Aurora borealis over Earth as seen from the International Space Station

better_than_last: This script incorporates the requested change to beat seven and ensures a seamless circular loop by ending on the current understanding of the solar wind, which flows back into its historical rejection.
